title: Can GPUs Continue To Dominate AI Compute?
gist: GPUs still hold 70% of installed worldwide AI compute capacity versus 30% for custom silicon, but OpenAI's newly benchmarked Jalapeño chip appears roughly competitive with Nvidia's Vera Rubin, and Google's TPU business is projected to hit $108 billion in revenue by 2028 — evidence that hyperscalers and frontier labs are converging on custom silicon as power and wafer scarcity make workload-specific chips economically rational.

themes.theme: Custom silicon share is rising fast against Nvidia

insights.claim: GPUs account for 70% of installed worldwide AI compute capacity by manufacturer, with custom silicon (primarily from Google and Amazon) making up the other 30%, per Epoch.ai data that excludes Meta, Microsoft, and Cerebras.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: The 70/30 split is the current baseline investors should track quarter to quarter as the clearest proxy for whether custom silicon is eating Nvidia's TAM.
insights.quote: GPUs are 70% of installed worldwide AI compute capacity by manufacturer (see figure 1), with custom silicon accounting for 30%, primarily Google and Amazon.

insights.claim: Installed AI compute capacity has grown 17X in three years; in 2023 Nvidia held 90% share and Google 10%, meaning custom AI compute has taken 20 percentage points of share from GPUs over that period.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A 20-point share shift in three years despite Nvidia's massive revenue growth shows share erosion can coexist with unit growth — don't infer GPU dominance is safe just because Nvidia's absolute revenue is still rising.
insights.quote: Installed AI compute capacity has grown 17X in three years. In 2023, Nvidia had 90% share and Google 10%. Custom AI compute took 20% share in the last 3 years.

insights.claim: The economics of building dedicated (rather than general-purpose) AI chips flipped in the last few years: a few years ago the incremental cost of developing two separate chips (~$100M+, including $30M+ for masks, tools and team) was prohibitive, but at today's installed-base scale it is affordable if the specialized chip delivers 10-30% better throughput/watt and 10-30% smaller silicon area — which matters because power and wafers are the scarcest resources in a supply-constrained environment likely to persist through 2030.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: This is the structural reason hyperscalers are now shipping separate training and inference chips (Google TPU 8t/8i, Meta MTIA variants) instead of one general chip — expect more workload-split silicon roadmaps through the rest of the decade.
insights.quote: at today's scales, it is affordable if the optimized chip can deliver 10% to 30% better throughput/watt with 10% to 30% smaller silicon area, because power and wafers are the scarcest resources in the constrained supply environment we are now in, which will likely persist through 2030.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'The scale of AI compute capacity'

insights.claim: Model makers and hyperscalers have a structural information advantage over GPU vendors: they know their own workload's split between training and inference, its bottlenecks, and their own strategic direction, and can run detailed benchmarks of their current silicon, planned features, and Nvidia silicon against their own huge installed compute base.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: This information asymmetry is a durable moat for custom silicon programs regardless of any single generation's benchmark results — it argues for a structural, not cyclical, shift away from merchant GPUs among the largest AI compute buyers.
insights.quote: They know their workloads better than the GPU vendors, they know the split between training and inference, and more importantly, they know the bottlenecks and their strategic direction.
insights.locator: section 'Do model makers have the edge'

themes.theme: Nvidia's moat: demand, systems integration, and capital

insights.claim: Jensen Huang said on Nvidia's August 26 earnings call/CNBC interview that demand is 'superstrong' and accelerating, Nvidia expects 70% growth in the coming fiscal year (limited by supply), and roughly half of Nvidia's business is hyperscalers with the other half spread across Neoclouds, Sovereign AI, and other buyers.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A diversified buyer base (half non-hyperscaler) partially insulates Nvidia from any single hyperscaler's custom-silicon defection, unlike a pure-hyperscaler-dependent model.
insights.quote: Nvidia expects 70% growth in the coming fiscal year (limited by supply)

insights.claim: Nvidia's edge is not just the GPU chip but a full integrated stack — NVL72 scale-up networking, racks, the Groq-derived LPU for low-latency inference, the agentic-optimized Vera CPU, BlueField DPU, and Spectrum-6 SPX scale-out networking — engineered together to deliver more performance than the GPU alone provides.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Investors should value Nvidia as a systems company, not a chip company — competitors matching GPU FLOPs alone (e.g., a bare custom ASIC) still face a networking/software integration gap.
insights.quote: All the pieces are engineered to work together and provide more performance boosts than what the GPU alone provides.

insights.claim: Nvidia's Vera CPU uses much larger single-threaded cores optimized for low-latency agentic AI workloads, delivering an estimated 1.8X performance improvement for agentic workloads versus a 'traditional' CPU.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Agentic workloads are becoming a distinct architectural target (latency-optimized CPU cores), a segment worth tracking separately from raw training/inference throughput benchmarks.
insights.quote: The company estimates this delivers 1.8X more performance for agentic workloads versus a 'traditional' CPU.

insights.claim: Nvidia's Vera Rubin NVL72 shows up to 30X better performance than GB300 on DeepSeek-v4-PRO at the highest-interactivity (most valuable) end of the workload curve, versus roughly 2X at lower interactivity — meaning the biggest generational gains land exactly where token-per-second-per-user value is highest.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Nvidia is deliberately steering its biggest performance gains toward the highest-value, most latency-sensitive inference segment, which is also where custom-silicon competitors like Jalapeño are targeting first — this is the key competitive battleground to watch.
insights.quote: Vera Rubin's advantage over GB300 is largest – up to 30X – where it is most valuable.

insights.claim: Nvidia is using its cash to lock in scarce supply: its supply commitments more than doubled from $119 billion to $279 billion per recent earnings-call disclosure, and its CFO said the projected 70% demand increase next year might be larger absent supply constraints.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A $279B supply commitment is a strong forward moat against custom-silicon competitors who must also compete for the same scarce TSMC wafers and HBM — capacity lock-in, not just chip design, is now a competitive weapon.
insights.quote: their supply commitments more than doubled from $119 billion to $279 billion

insights.claim: Nvidia has invested in open-weight models (Nemotron takes 3 of the top 4 slots in OpenRouter's most-used free models) and did a $7 billion deal with Poolside to license its open-weight model software and hire over 100 of its engineers, even though free models don't directly make Nvidia money.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Nvidia is buying model-layer insight and customer engagement to defend its hardware moat against model-maker-led custom silicon — a $7B bet signals Jensen sees the model layer as strategically necessary, not just adjacent.
insights.quote: Free models don't make Nvidia money, so Jensen must see value in the insight they provide and the customer engagement they generate.

themes.theme: OpenAI's Jalapeño and the model-maker silicon race

insights.claim: OpenAI's first chip, Jalapeño, was developed in a short timeframe by a small team (led by Google TPU alumni Richard Ho, Ravi Narayanaswami, and Chris Leary) heavily augmented by OpenAI's own AI coding tools, and it outperformed Nvidia's GB300 by a significant amount across GPT-OSS, DeepSeek R1, and Kimi K2.5 benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A small team building a chip that beats a market leader's flagship in under two years — using AI tools themselves — signals design-cycle time for custom AI silicon is compressing, lowering the barrier for other frontier labs to follow.
insights.quote: Jalapeño, OpenAI's first chip, is very impressive, as were presenters Richard Ho, Ravi Narayanaswami, and Chris Leary (notably, all three of them are Google TPU alumni).

insights.claim: Jalapeño's benchmarks so far use only single-token prediction (STP); OpenAI plans to apply multi-token prediction (MTP) in the future, which the author expects to boost performance a further 3 to 5X.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: If MTP delivers the claimed 3-5X on top of already GB300-beating STP results, Jalapeño's real-world performance gap over Nvidia could widen substantially once deployed — a leading indicator to watch in OpenAI's Gen2 announcements.
insights.quote: They will apply MTP (multi-token prediction) in the future, which will boost performance 3 to 5X.

insights.claim: By roughly shifting the Nvidia GB300-to-Vera-Rubin performance curve (2X to 30X depending on interactivity) onto the Jalapeño-vs-GB300 results, the author estimates Jalapeño is roughly competitive with Vera Rubin — a guesstimate later corroborated when SemiAnalysis published analysis estimating Jalapeño goes head-to-head with Vera Rubin.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: If a chip built by a first-time entrant with a small team truly matches Nvidia's next-gen flagship, that is the single most important competitive signal in this piece — it directly threatens the 'GPUs are unmatched' thesis.
insights.quote: Following Hot Chips, SemiAnalysis published its analysis and estimated Jalapeño appears to go head-to-head with Vera Rubin.
insights.locator: paragraph on Jalapeño vs Vera Rubin comparison

insights.claim: Jalapeño cannot help with model training — probably over a third of OpenAI's total compute needs — so OpenAI will keep buying/renting GPU training capacity even as it scales Jalapeño for inference; the author flags that if Jalapeño holds up in production it would be 'a big warning sign for GPUs.'
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: The GPU threat from Jalapeño is inference-specific, not existential to training demand — investors should model Nvidia's training-chip revenue separately from its (more exposed) inference-chip revenue when assessing OpenAI's custom silicon impact.
insights.quote: If Jalapeño turns out in production deployment to be as good (or better) than Vera Rubin, that will be a big warning sign for GPUs.

insights.claim: Nvidia invested $30 billion in OpenAI not long before OpenAI unveiled a chip (Jalapeño) that appears to directly compete with Nvidia's own Vera Rubin.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Highlights a structural conflict of interest/coopetition dynamic: Nvidia is financing a customer that is simultaneously building silicon to reduce its GPU dependence — worth watching for how this shapes future Nvidia-OpenAI supply and investment terms.
insights.quote: Interestingly, Nvidia invested $30 Billion in OpenAI not long ago.

insights.claim: Anthropic has hired Clive Chan, a key member of OpenAI's hardware team, and publicly confirmed it is building an in-house silicon team to design custom chips for Claude, describing it as 'the latest step in our multi-chip approach.'
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A third major frontier lab (after Google and OpenAI) is now building dedicated silicon — reinforces that custom AI chips are becoming table stakes for any frontier model maker with enough compute scale, not a one-off strategy.
insights.quote: Anthropic has publicly confirmed recently that it's building an in-house silicon team to design custom chips for Claude, calling it 'the latest step in our multi-chip approach.'
insights.locator: section 'Anthropic is building its own AI compute chip team'

insights.claim: Google has done AI compute for 10 years (TPU #1 in 2015 for inference, TPU #2 for training) and has historically alternated optimizing between training and inference each generation; with TPU 8t (training) and 8i (inference) it is now launching both simultaneously, each delivering roughly double the performance of the previous TPU generation.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Simultaneous dual-chip launches confirm Google's AI compute business has crossed the scale threshold where workload-specific optimization pays for itself — a template other hyperscalers (and OpenAI) appear to be following.
insights.quote: Now Google is launching TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference at the same time.

insights.claim: TPU 8i (inference) is about 1.4X the physical size of TPU 8t (training) due to more HBM; the author estimates a single chip doing both training and inference well would need to be another 10-20% larger than TPU 8i to add all the back-propagation logic needed for training.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Quantifies the silicon-area savings from splitting training/inference chips (roughly 10-20%+ smaller each versus a unified design) — a concrete number for modeling why hyperscalers are moving to split architectures.
insights.quote: A single chip that does both inference and training well would probably be another 10% to 20% larger than TPU 8i to add all the back-propagation logic needed for training.

insights.claim: Google uses different interconnect topologies for inference versus training: inference uses 'Boardfly' (fully-connected trays/groups via optical circuit switches, max 7 hops, 1,152 TPU 8i's) to minimize latency, while training uses a traditional 3D torus with higher bisection bandwidth (up to 16 hops, up to 9,600 TPU 8t's per superpod via OCS), and the Virgo Network scales this to a non-blocking fabric of up to 134,400 TPUs for the largest frontier models.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Optical circuit switching (OCS) is presented as Google's core structural advantage over copper-based scale-out networking — a differentiator Nvidia/AMD would need to match architecturally, not just match on chip FLOPs.
insights.quote: Google has developed the Virgo Network to provide a global non-blocking cluster fabric for up to 134,400 TPUs for the largest frontier models.

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley estimates Google's TPU sales will be $9 billion in the second half of 2026, growing to $84 billion in 2027 and $108 billion in 2028 — comparable in scale to Nvidia's most recent quarterly revenue of $96 billion (projected $108 billion next quarter, ~90% of it data-center revenue).
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: If accurate, Google's TPU external sales alone would reach roughly Nvidia's current single-quarter revenue run rate by 2028 — a hard revenue number for modeling custom silicon's dollar-for-dollar displacement of GPU spend.
insights.quote: Morgan Stanley recently estimated Google's sales of TPUs will be $9 billion in the second half of this year, $84 billion in 2027, and $108 billion in 2028.

insights.claim: Major TPU users include Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, and Apple — meaning some of Nvidia's largest customers/competitors are also buying compute from Google's custom silicon rather than exclusively GPUs.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Cross-buying of TPUs by frontier labs that are simultaneously building their own chips (OpenAI, Anthropic) shows compute sourcing is now genuinely multi-vendor even at the top of the market, diluting any single vendor's pricing power.
insights.quote: Major TPU users include Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, and Apple.

themes.theme: Other custom accelerators and GPU-maker countermoves

insights.claim: AMD's MI455x GPU and Helios rack-scale system use a 72-GPU scale-up domain built on Broadcom Ethernet switches; AMD has grown its worldwide installed AI-compute share from 0% to 6%, but did not provide a performance chart for any AI workload at Hot Chips.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: The absence of a performance benchmark from AMD at a showcase event is itself a signal — it suggests AMD's competitive position versus Vera Rubin/Jalapeño is weaker than its share gains imply, worth scrutinizing in AMD's next earnings commentary.
insights.quote: AMD has come a very long way in a relatively short time and has grown worldwide installed share from 0% to 6%. Unfortunately, it did not provide a performance chart for any AI workload.

insights.claim: Meta's MTIA accelerators are purpose-built because Meta says GPUs are poorly suited to its recommendation-system workloads (terabytes of sparse embedding tables, memory-bound operations); MTIA 300 already shows slightly higher performance/$ than GPUs for large-batch training, and MTIA 400 is in development for both GenAI and recommendation systems, with a new chip roughly every six months.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Meta's recommendation-system workload is fundamentally different from LLM training/inference, showing custom silicon's advantage is not limited to frontier-model compute — any hyperscaler with a distinct, large-scale workload has an economic case for its own chip.
insights.quote: It is now showing slightly higher performance/$ for large batch training than GPUs.

insights.claim: Cerebras announced CS-4, offering 2X faster tokens/user than CS-3 and up to 10X throughput/watt of CS-3; the company says CS-5 will double performance again in a year and CS-6 will double again the year after with 3D stacked DRAM.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: If Cerebras hits its stated CS-5/CS-6 roadmap, it becomes an increasingly credible low-latency alternative for the highest-value inference segment Nvidia is also targeting with Vera Rubin — worth tracking against actual delivered (not just announced) performance.
insights.quote: the company says CS-5 will double performance again in a year, then CS-6 another doubling the year after that with 3D stacked DRAM!

insights.claim: The author suggests AMD could consider buying Cerebras (whose market cap is about 1/10th of AMD's) or an AI-compute startup like Etched to acquire a low-latency inference solution comparable to Nvidia's Groq-derived LPU.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: A speculative but concrete M&A idea — an AMD-Cerebras deal would be a notable consolidation event in the low-latency inference niche and is worth flagging as a scenario for AMD-related event-driven positioning.
insights.quote: AMD might consider buying Cerebras (whose market cap is 1/10th of AMD's) to provide an LPX-like solution for customers wanting very low-latency inferencing.
insights.locator: section 'What more can GPU makers do'

insights.claim: Copper interconnects are reaching their performance limit, so further GPU performance gains will require optical interconnects; hyperscalers are expected to adopt the lower-risk NPO (near-package optics) first even though it cannot match the performance ceiling of CPO (co-packaged optics), giving Nvidia/AMD an opening to integrate CPO early for a performance edge competitors using NPO/copper cannot match. The author discloses he is a board member at both an OCS company and an optical engine company.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: Given the author's disclosed board positions in optical-interconnect companies, treat the CPO-over-NPO prediction as informed but potentially self-interested — still, it flags optical interconnects (CPO specifically) as a likely next differentiation battleground for GPU vendors.
insights.quote: Copper interconnects are reaching their limit. GPU performance increases will require optical interconnects.

themes.theme: Where each hyperscaler's compute demand actually goes

insights.claim: The author's framework for judging custom-silicon risk to Nvidia/AMD is ownership structure of compute demand: Anthropic's and OpenAI's workloads are 100% their own; Google's and Meta's workloads are probably majority their own; Amazon's and Microsoft's workloads are mostly their (external cloud) customers'.
insights.speaker: Geoff Tate
insights.so_what: This is a practical screen for gauging which hyperscalers can most easily substitute their own silicon for Nvidia GPUs without needing to convince third-party customers — Anthropic/OpenAI/Google/Meta are the highest-risk names for Nvidia's inference/training revenue, Amazon/Microsoft less so given customer-driven demand.
insights.quote: Anthropic and OpenAI workloads are 100% their own. Google's and Meta's workloads are probably a majority their own. Amazon's and Microsoft's workloads are mostly their customers'.
